                                      ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
A book this packed doesn’t just spring into being. It’s a combination of a lot of hard work by the two of us, and a lot
of help and encouragement from a whole bunch of people. On behalf of Thomas, I want to thank some of them.
	 Some years ago, I started revealing the magicians’ secrets of puzzlemaking. (So far, the puzzlemakers’ union hasn’t
threatened me with a real-life game of hangman.) I first spelled out the basics of puzzlemaking in a two-article series
in Dragon magazine. Editor Dave Gross was instrumental in making that concept accessible to readers, and helping
define the how-to style that I would make a trademark of my columns.
	The Dragon pieces were so well received that I approached Games magazine about writing a series called
Puzzlecraft. This column, molded by editors R. Wayne Schmittberger, Susan West, and Jennifer Orehowsky, would
break down the basics of a puzzle type each month. I imagined I could get maybe a dozen articles out of that. We got
up to 100 articles before we retired the series in 2014.
	 My wife, Evon Fuerst, gets a special acknowledgment for that. When the Games column was in its mid-40s and
entering a midlife crisis, she suggested I get a coauthor, specifically Thomas “Dr. Sudoku” Snyder, a bioengineering
researcher who made his name as a puzzle champion. I called him in as my coauthor on Puzzlecraft, and later as my
collaborator in bringing the Decode puzzle site to life for Wired magazine. Marrying Evon and getting Thomas as
a collaborator seem to prove that I can make good decisions when I try hard enough.
	 At Puzzlewright Press, editors Francis Heaney and Peter Gordon worked with us to take these concepts from
article form into a holistically designed book. (And Francis drew some very nice pictures of us.) They encouraged us
to write all-new puzzles, with the goal of not being boxed in by puzzles clearly designed for magazine presentation.
We gave the book words, and they gave it wings. Francis came back to edit this second edition, for which I am most
grateful.
	 Along the way, we had many great test-solvers. Jeffrey L. Harris was the tester for many of the articles in Games,
and this book’s puzzles were tested by Chris and Sora Battey, Carrie and Nick Emmerich, Dan Feyer, Wei-Hwa Huang,
Sylvia Luxembourg, Julia Sabin, Mike Sylvia, Matt Tabak, Sean Trowbridge, Jason Wodicka, and Wil Zambole. We’d
also be remiss if we didn’t thank the letter writers who gave us feedback on our columns over the years.
	 I’ve been fortunate to work with the best puzzlemakers in the world, many of whom are mentioned in this book.
I’m indebted to Martin Gardner, Will Shortz, Dan Katz, Mark L. Gottlieb, Mike Shenk, Teeuwynn Woodruff, Stanley
Newman, Eric Harshbarger, Scott Kim, Ken Jennings, Elan Lee, Cliff Johnson, Jordan Weisman, Elisa Teague, Jeff
Martin, and many others for working with me on each of these puzzle types for one project or another. They got to
see the versions with all the errors. Lucky them.
	 At Lone Shark Games, Gaby Weidling has been the throughline for most of our puzzle projects, and developed
the second edition of this book. The team of Chad Brown, Trevor Kidd, Sean Molley, Tanis O’Connor, Paul Peterson,
Keith Richmond, Aviva Schecterson, Liz Spain, Shane Steed, Rodney Thompson, and Skylar Woodies helped make
this a Lone Shark book worthy of standing next to The Maze of Games. Quizmaster Peter Sagal wrote an illuminat-
ing foreword. Tiffany Chatham Smith of Regent Publishing assembled this book into the amazing form it’s in now.
Kelley Allen, Dana Williams, and everyone at Humble Bundle helped us spring the new edition on an unsuspecting
world.
	 Finally, there’s my mom, Phyllis Selinker. Other than the obvious, she did two things that radically influenced
the direction of this book. First, she encouraged me to submit my puzzles to Games and Dragon when I was 13, and
second, she stopped me from dropping out of high school when I proved I could make a living at it. Well, maybe I
hadn’t proved it to her. I’ll bet I have now, though.
	 And of course, thanks to you for being a puzzlecrafter. We hope you enjoy torturing solvers as much as we do.
                                                                                                      —Mike Selinker
                                                                                                  Seattle, Washington
                                                                                                          August 2018

                                   23 THE BLANKEST PLACE ON EARTH
Alice in Wonderland: Alice chases the White Rabbit into a hole and gets trapped in Wonderland, where the Cheshire
Cat appears as a smile, the Mad Hatter celebrates his unbirthday, and the Queen of Hearts aims to cut off her head.
[In a coincidence of Carrollian proportions, “March Hare” also fits alphabetically in the blanks for “Mad Hatter.”
A tip of our (in this style 10/6) hat to you if you found both solutions.]
Fantasia: A series of classical compositions accompany Mickey Mouse battling enchanted broomsticks, an alligator
dancing with a hippo, and the demon Chernabog raging atop Bald Mountain.
Finding Nemo: A clownfish named Nemo gets lost in the Great Barrier Reef, but with the help of an amnesiac fish
named Dory, he is reunited with his father Marlin.
Frozen: Queen Elsa plunges the kingdom of Arendelle into eternal winter, but her sister Anna joins with an iceman
named Kristoff, his reindeer Sven, and the snowman Olaf to reverse the spell.
Inside Out: An adolescent girl suffers mood swings after her family moves to San Francisco. Her emotions—Joy,
Sadness, Fear, Disgust, and Anger—try to keep her from running away. Also, she has an imaginary friend named
Bing Bong.
The Lion King: After his father Mufasa’s death, the young lion Simba is tricked into giving up his throne by his uncle
Scar. Aided by a warthog, a meerkat, and a wise monkey, he returns with his mate Nala to take his place in the “Circle
of Life.”
The Little Mermaid: When the mermaid Ariel falls in love with a prince named Eric, a witch gives her legs in
exchange for her voice. After Ursula is defeated, King Triton permits his daughter to stay above the sea.
One Hundred and One Dalmatians: A pair of Dalmatians has its litter of fifteen puppies stolen by the villainous
Cruella De Vil, who wants to turn them into coats. They rescue an additional eighty-four dogs, and adopt them all.
Peter Pan: Peter Pan coaxes the Darling children to fly toward the “Second Star to the Right” to reach Never Land.
They join with the Lost Boys and the fairy Tinker Bell to fight off Captain Hook and his band of pirates.
Pinocchio: When the woodworker Geppetto makes a wish upon a star, a marionette named Pinocchio comes to life
and later becomes a real boy.
Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs: The princess Snow White is hidden from an evil queen by seven dwarfs—Doc,
Grumpy, Happy, Sleepy, Bashful, Sneezy, and Dopey. She is poisoned, but a handsome prince comes along and
awakens her with a kiss.
WALL•E: The trash-compactor robot WALL•E is visited by the probe EVE, who searches for life on the planet Earth.
They save the last plant from a spaceship’s autopilot and guide the humans back to repopulate their home.


                     25 WIKIPEDIA BLACK AND THE CASE OF THE MISSING LINKS
Wikipedia identified Dr. Fassel as the accomplice. He stated the word “brontosaurus” was really another name for
the apatosaurus, but that idea went extinct in 2015 when paleontologists agreed that the brontosaur was of a different
genus. Armed with Wikipedia’s revelation, Chief Black discovered that “Dr.” Fassel had faked his own credentials to
get a chance at stealing the museum’s fossil collection. Cookie Crook remains at large.



                                                                                                                229
                                               27 QUADRI-LATERALS
Operator Error: Doctor Dave is a veterinarian, and the kid is his goat.
Death in the Elevator: The man with the basement office was one of the building’s superintendents. He turned off
the elevators because the doors were malfunctioning. He opened the hatch at the top of the elevator to see if there
was something wrong with the mechanism. Sadly, that was when the businessman, checking his cell phone, walked
out of his 30th-floor office, directly past the warning tape, and through the malfunctioning elevator doors—where
there was no elevator. He fell 30 stories, right into the open hatch, crushing the superintendent.
Bucky Gets Lucky: Lucky is a jockey, and his horse crossed the finish line a fraction of a second before he did.
The President’s Precedent: The year is 1796. Samuel Johnston, who was born in Scotland and moved to North Caro-
lina as a child, was allowed to run because the Constitution says, “No person except a natural born Citizen, or a Citizen
of the United States, at the time of the Adoption of this Constitution, shall be eligible to the Office of President.”
Johnston was a citizen when the Constitution was ratified. Needless to say, this loophole is not exploitable today.
Albatross Soup (extra puzzle from Lateral Thinking section): The man had previously crashed his boat on a desert
island. One friend had died, but he and his other friend struggled to stay alive. One day, the friend offered him “albatross
soup,” which he ate. After being rescued, the man went to the restaurant and had the albatross soup, which didn’t taste
anything like what he expected. The man then knew he had been given the dead man’s remains, and couldn’t live with
that knowledge. (See? Creepy.)

                                                   71 LIPTOGRAMS
	1.	 Make your selection of a good quotation to utilize not just based on what you favor but on what will vex your
   solvers most
	2.	 Adjust your plaintext keeping firmly in mind that qualities like word size can give away answers
	3.	 Pick a method of ciphertexting that does the job to move your message toward realization
	4.	 Transmogrify cryptogrammatically jockeying betwixt the original words and the subsequent puzzle
	5.	 Seize the opportunity to expertly double check for misjudgments which might’ve been quickly introduced
	6.	 Compose a finished working version and enjoy your baffled friends’ quizzical expressions
The missing letters from the lipograms are P, B, Q, V, A, and T. These can be rot-13ed to CODING.

                                191 THE DEATH OF DR. ZERO                                                            3   4   0
         To start, it helps to realize the properties of the set of robots and each bit. Based                       3   1   3
         on the first bit, only two could be the killer robot (000 and 001), but the third bit                       3       3
         separates these two into 000, who could kill a human, and 001, who must kill all                            3   0   4
         humans. So at the end of this murder mystery, 001 will be revealed as the killer,                           1   6   4
         but which robot is 001?
         	 The easiest robots to identify are 111, who always tells the truth, and 101, who                          1 6 6 6 6
         always lies. 111 will say it is not the killer and 101 will say that it is. Of the two                      1       6
         choices for 101 (Delta and Omega), Omega can be excluded, as its third state-                               0       2
         ment would not be false. So Delta is 101, which tells us that Gamma is not 111,                             0 2 2 2 2
         as Delta’s third statement is false. That leaves Alpha and Beta as potential 111s,
                                                                                                                     0   2   1
         but Alpha’s statement about having a middle 0 would be a lie, so Beta is 111.
         	 Beta’s third statement tells us Alpha is 100 or 001, but if Alpha were 001 then                           5   5   1
         it couldn’t say it had a 0 as its middle number, so Alpha is 100. This leaves 000                           5 5 5 1 1
         and 001 for Gamma and Omega; the killer (001) would say it was innocent, so
         Omega is 000—leaving Gamma as 001, the killer robot.

                                              206 CRAWL OF FAME
	1.	Ike was inducted into the World Golf Hall of Fame.
	2.	Golfer Gary Player’s last name can be curtailed and anagrammed to the last name of CBS chief executive
   William S. Paley, who is in the Television Academy Hall of Fame.
	3.	Actor Danny Thomas’s first name anagrams to the last letters of the doll Raggedy Ann, who is in the National
   Toy Hall of Fame.
	4.	Her brother Raggedy Andy entered the same year as the kite, which got inventor Benjamin Franklin into the
   Electrostatics Hall of Fame.
	5.	The last word of physicist Robert J. Van de Graaff ’s name can be reduced to the last name of tennis star Steffi
   Graf, who is in the Tennis Hall of Fame.
	6.	Tennis star Chris Evert has a horse named after her in the National Museum of Racing and Hall of Fame.
	7.	Chris Evert (the horse) was a filly, a homonym of the first word in the name of the Phillie Phanatic, a member
   of the Mascot Hall of Fame.
	8.	The University of Tennessee’s bluetick coonhound Smokey shares a name with singer Smokey Robinson, who
   is in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
	9.	Robinson’s backup singers, the Miracles, can lose the last letter of “Miracles” to become Miracle, a film about
   Miracle on Ice coach Herb Brooks, who is in the Hockey Hall of Fame.
	10.	 NHL chairman Harley Hotchkiss’s first name is the last name of Harley-Davidson founder William S. Harley,
   who is in the Motorcycle Hall of Fame.
	11.	 Motorcycle stuntman Evel Knievel’s name contains the same unique letters as actor Kevin Kline, who is in the
   American Theater Hall of Fame.
	12.	 Actresses Ethel Barrymore and Ethel Merman’s last names can be combined to the last name of broadcaster
   Chris Berman, who received the Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award from the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
	13.	 Defensive end David Jones, better known as Deacon Jones, can have “slate” added phonetically to his common
      nickname so that it is pronounced as the name of astronaut Deke Slayton, who is in the United States
      Astronaut Hall of Fame.
	14.	 Astronaut Sally Ride’s last name can replace its even letters with numbers to become Star Wars character
      R2-D2, who is in the Robot Hall of Fame.
	15.	 The robot ASIMO can have a V added to make the last name of author Isaac Asimov, who is in the Science
      Fiction and Fantasy Hall of Fame.
	16.	 Author A.E. van Vogt’s initials can be shifted to those of ringmaster P.T. Barnum, who is in the Circus Hall of
      Fame.
	17.	 Western star Tom Mix’s name ends in the Roman numeral for 2009. His name rhymes with “comics,” which is
      the subject of the Will Eisner Comic Book Hall of Fame.
	18.	 Comic artist Wally Wood’s name rhymes with your destination: HOLLYWOOD.

                                   217 STORY TIME AT THE HORNER HOUSE
Papa Bear uses 1940 police CB radio code (“Papa bear” is CB slang for a police officer), known as ten-code. Each
coded statement has an associated 10-X number (e.g., “10-4”); the text, which was Caesar shifted by 10 to encode
it, reads: “Return to your station • Stand by until no interference • Repeat, conditions bad • Pick up a prisoner at
• Relay.” These correspond to 10-19, 10-23, 10-9, 10-14, and 10-5. Those numbers alphanumerically spell SWIPE.
Mama Bear has room for a letter between two occurrences of “MA” in each answer: “Lady Marmalade” (R), Mau-Mau
(U), Mamma Mia! (M), The Mapmaker’s Daughter (P), Animal Magnetism (L), Mae Marsh (E), and Mad Max (D).
Those letters spell RUMPLED.
Baby Bear likes Chicago Cubs players whose last names can be indexed by the numbering of positions in scorecard-
keeping. They are 3B Steve Buechele (5 = H), SS Rey Sánchez (6 = E), P Grover Cleveland Alexander (1 = A),
LF Jimmy Sheckard (7 = R), RF Phil Cavarretta (9 = T), CF José Cardenal (8 = L), C Gabby Hartnett (2 = A), 1B Ernie
Banks (3 = N), and 2B Ryne Sandberg (4 = D); the indexed letters spell HEARTLAND.
The Three Bears join SWIPE and RUMPLED, in which they have embedded a HEARTLAND (that is, a land at the
center). In the heart of “swiPERUmpled” is the answer: PERU.
The Pig in the House of Straw is eating berries. Like the word “straw,” each answer can go before “berry” to make a
fruit: elder, Logan, Goose, tea, Blue, and rasp. The indicated letters spell EASTER.
The Pig in the House of Sticks combines the tiered fourths of the four nautical flags that represent the letters in
NAVY.
The Pig in the House of Bricks needs to gather his bricks and put them in the wall in this order: winner, confine,
dating, insect, speech, hurriedly, and eyeball. This makes clues to the answers Adrien, detain, Tinder, red ant, tirade,
dart in, and retina. Each is missing one letter (in order) from the word TRAINED.
The Three Little Pigs’ answers, EASTER, NAVY, and TRAINED, can all precede SEAL.
